claims.claim: Academic vocabulary is the vocabulary used in academic contexts — spoken contexts such as lectures, seminars, and presentations, and written contexts such as essays, articles, and reports.

Academic vocabulary can be understood as three kinds of words: general words used academically, non-general academic words that recur across disciplines, and technical words specific to an individual subject.

Researchers have built lists (the academic-word-list idea) of words that are not common enough to be learned through ordinary study but are frequent across most academic disciplines; these words can be studied by all learners of academic English.
Some common general words carry special meanings in academic contexts, such as population (the group a study samples) and discipline (a subject of study).
Academic English is a formal, written style: it uses formal vocabulary (including words from academic word lists) and avoids less formal or idiomatic vocabulary.
Formal academic style prefers single-word verbs to two-word (phrasal) verbs, and full verb forms to contractions (do not, cannot, will not rather than don't, can't, won't).

Hedging (cautious or tentative language) makes claims less absolute using modals such as may and might, adverbs such as possibly, and cautious verbs such as appears to and seems to; it keeps writers from presenting conclusions as facts.

Formal language is used in serious situations and is more common in writing; informal language is more common in relaxed situations and in speech, and contractions are more common in informal language.

More formal vocabulary commonly involves longer words, often with origins in Latin and Greek, while more informal vocabulary commonly involves shorter words, often with Anglo-Saxon origins (for example commence/start, terminate/end).

The level of formality in writing should be determined by the expectations of the audience and the purpose; a college academic essay calls for a formal style, while a letter to a friend calls for an informal style.
Affect is a verb meaning to influence or cause someone or something to change; effect is a noun meaning the result of an influence.
A speaker implies — puts a suggestion into a message — while a listener infers — takes a suggestion out of a message; infer commonly pairs with the preposition from.

A word family is a group of words related by a common base word and formed by adding prefixes or suffixes (create, creator, creativity, creation, creative, creatively); studying word families helps learners build vocabulary more quickly.

A collocation is two or more words that frequently appear together, with types such as adjective+noun and verb+noun (examples drawn from academic collocation lists); collocations are a feature of academic vocabulary worth studying.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Whether the 'avoid contractions' and 'avoid phrasal verbs' conventions are absolute rules of academic writing.
positions: Formal style guidance (Purdue OWL, EAP Foundation, Cambridge Grammar) directs writers to prefer full verb forms, single-word verbs, and formal vocabulary in academic writing.
Some contemporary academic genres and journals accept contractions and phrasal verbs, especially in less formal academic settings such as discussion posts or blog-style writing.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson presents these conventions as general guidelines of the formal register — choices driven by audience and purpose — rather than as absolute laws, and it uses its own original examples throughout.

unsupportedExistingClaims: The machine-generated draft described academic vocabulary only as 'a foundational Languages & ESL concept' and 'a building block for later discussions,' with no register, precision, hedging, or formality content; that boilerplate was discarded.

sourceRecords.title: Using Appropriate Language — Purdue OWL
sourceRecords.notes: Tier A. Read live on 2026-08-21 (HTTP 200). Supports: language should fit the audience and match the purpose; levels of formality as a key consideration; avoidance of slang and idiomatic expressions in general academic writing; jargon reserved for in-group audiences. Reference only; prose synthesized.

sourceRecords.title: Levels of Formality — Purdue OWL
sourceRecords.notes: Tier A. Read live on 2026-08-21 (HTTP 200). Supports: the level of formality is determined by the expectations of the audience and the purpose; a college academic essay is written in a formal style; formality exists on a scale with semi-formal registers between the poles. Reference only; prose synthesized.

sourceRecords.title: Academic vocabulary — EAP Foundation
sourceRecords.notes: Tier B. Read live on 2026-08-21 (HTTP 200). Supports: academic vocabulary as the vocabulary usable in academic contexts (lectures, seminars, presentations; essays, articles, reports); the three-type model (general words used academically, non-general academic words, technical words); the rationale for research-based academic word lists (words not common enough for ordinary study but frequent across disciplines); special academic meanings of general words (discipline, population, control); the importance of academic tone in word choice. Reference only; prose synthesized.

sourceRecords.title: Academic Style — EAP Foundation
sourceRecords.notes: Tier B. Read live on 2026-08-21 (HTTP 200). Supports: academic English as a formal written style distinct from spoken academic English; formal vocabulary (including academic-word-list words) over casual or idiomatic vocabulary; single-word formal verbs over two-word verbs (increase/discuss vs go up/talk about); full verb forms over contractions (do not vs don't); precision over vague words such as 'thing'; hedging with may, might, possibly, appears to, seems to to avoid absolute statements. Reference only; prose synthesized.

sourceRecords.title: Hedging (cautious language) — EAP Foundation
sourceRecords.notes: Tier B. Read live on 2026-08-21 (HTTP 200). Supports: hedging as a way of softening language by making claims or conclusions less absolute; its use in the sciences (hypotheses, results) and other disciplines to avoid presenting conclusions or ideas as facts and to distance the writer from claims; modal verbs, introductory verbs, adverbs, adjectives, and nouns as hedging devices. Reference only; prose synthesized.

sourceRecords.title: Features of vocabulary — EAP Foundation
sourceRecords.notes: Tier B. Read live on 2026-08-21 (HTTP 200). Supports: word families as groups of words related by a common base word and formed with prefixes/suffixes (create, creator, creativity, creation, creative, creatively), with faster vocabulary growth as the benefit; collocations as two or more words that frequently appear together, with types such as adjective+noun and verb+noun drawn from the Academic Collocation List; register as a feature of vocabulary important for academic (formal) English; phrasal verbs as multi-word verbs that form a single unit rather than true collocations. Reference only; prose synthesized.

sourceRecords.title: Formal and informal language — Cambridge Dictionary (English Grammar Today)
sourceRecords.notes: Tier B. Read live on 2026-08-21 (HTTP 200). Supports: formal language in serious situations and with people not well known, informal language in relaxed situations with people well known; formal language more common when writing and informal more common when speaking; contractions as more common in informal language; formal vocabulary commonly involving longer words with Latin or Greek origins versus informal shorter words with Anglo-Saxon origins (commence/start, terminate/end); modal verbs (may, might) as more formal and polite choices. Reference only; all lesson examples original.

sourceRecords.title: Affect or effect? — Cambridge Dictionary (English Grammar Today)
sourceRecords.notes: Tier B. Read live on 2026-08-21 (HTTP 200). Supports: affect as a verb meaning to influence or cause someone or something to change; effect as a noun meaning the result of an influence. The lesson uses its own original example sentences for this pair. Reference only.

sourceRecords.title: Imply or infer? — Cambridge Dictionary (English Grammar Today)
sourceRecords.notes: Tier B. Read live on 2026-08-21 (HTTP 200). Supports: a speaker can imply (put a suggestion into the message) but a listener can only infer (take the suggestion out of the message); infer is used with the preposition from; the typical error of using infer for what someone has said. The lesson uses original example sentences. Reference only.
